reason: The line holds, but one of the two witnesses the verifier leaned on does not say what the verifier says it says, so the evidence is thinner than claimed and the note should carry a caveat. (1) THE EVIDENCE CLAIM IS WRONG IN PART. The evidence field says the Rachel Carson page at Wikiquote and a Brain Pickings essay "agree on all three sentences in this order, including the definite article in spring after the winter". I read Wikiquote. Its entry is one sentence only, "Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts.", sourced to The Sense of Wonder (1965); the second and third sentences are not in that entry at all, and the neighbouring entry is the separate "Those who dwell, as scientists or laymen" passage. Wikiquote therefore corroborates the attribution and the first sentence, and nothing about the birds, the tides, the folded bud, the em dash or the definite article. (2) THE WORDING SURVIVES ANYWAY. The Marginalian essay I fetched returns all three sentences in order, verbatim as proposed: "Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts. There is symbolic as well as actual beauty in the migration of the birds, the ebb and flow of the tides, the folded bud ready for the spring. There is something infinitely healing in the repeated refrains of nature — the assurance that dawn comes after night, and spring after the winter." A second, independent reproduction returns the same three sentences and confirms the definite article, spring after the winter, which is the reading most short web copies drop. So the shipped wording exists in reproductions of the named book and nothing is minted. (3) ONE CHARACTER REMAINS OPEN, and the note should say so: the comma before "and spring after the winter". The Marginalian prints it; other reproductions run the clause on without it. The em dash spacing differs the same way, spaced on the web and closed up in the proposal, which is ordinary Harper and Row setting and not a wording question; the corpus already carries seven quotations with an em dash, so the mark itself is precedented and the rule against dashes binds only the source and the note. I could not settle the comma: both archive.org copies of The Sense of Wonder are lending-restricted and the plain-text route returns the item-not-available page, and the Oberlin PDF on the text's provenance is a scan with no extractable text. (4) LOCATOR. Independent sources place the passage at the end of the book, one of them saying in as many words that The Sense of Wonder ends with it. The source says only "the closing paragraph", which is where the sentences sit; it does not claim to be the whole paragraph, and the paragraph opens with the "Those who dwell, as scientists or laymen" sentences. Sound. (5) ATTRIBUTION, SCOPE, FORM. Carson's own prose, no speaker, on none of the misattribution rows. The Sense of Wonder (Harper and Row, 1965) is the book made from Help Your Child to Wonder, Woman's Home Companion, July 1956, so pre-1999 and a named work; Essay is the right tag and matches the Thoreau, Dillard and Twain precedents; publishable; on the theme. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Carson 0 of 3, not banned, and there is no second Carson in the April verdict list. Source line leads with the name, 80 characters, no dash, no straight double quote, and the quotation ends in a full stop. WHAT I ASK OF THE EDITOR: keep the Marginalian reading, comma and all, and let the note say plainly that the printed page was not seen and that reproductions differ over that one comma.
